documents.title: Generative AI (guidance incl. 'Adhere to the Academic Policy')
documents.summary: The Office of Information Technology page gives Institute-wide generative AI guidance: encourages thoughtful use, points to school and instructor rules for academic use, and sets security, privacy, accuracy and vendor-review expectations. It has no tiers or templates.
documents.stance_why: The page says Georgia Tech "encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI" but sets no course-level rule: it tells readers to "Examine the handbooks and policies of your respective College and School" and tells faculty to "communicate explicitly" with students. It sets no stance of its own and hands the decision to schools and instructors, so delegates.

units.why: Definition sentence: "refers to a category of AI capable of analyzing and emulating datasets" sets what the guidance covers, so it is a scope definition (P61, informs, general), not a rule.

units.frag_start: Generative AI, or GenAI for short
units.frag_end: code in response to given inputs or instructions

units.why: "Georgia Tech encourages the thoughtful use of Gen AI technologies" states a default of welcoming AI use; it is a stance (P02) rather than a framework, though P56 also fits, because it says AI use is encouraged.

units.why: "Schools will revise and formulate new policies" says the guidance is interim and policy will change as understanding grows, which is P54 (revisit), stated as a fact so modality is informs.

units.why: "Remain vigilant against phishing" with the statement that GenAI makes phishing emails and "deepfakes" easier names a harm of AI; harms are P53, stated as fact (informs). The security-practice advice is a separate unit.

units.resolution_why: A coded the phishing sentence as informs and split off the reporting directive; B merged both into one should unit. The sentence naming the harm ("simplified the process for malevolent individuals to craft advanced phishing emails") is a fact, so informs; the directive is a separate rule and is kept as its own unit (see next).

units.why: "adhere to security best practices and to report any dubious messages" is a security reporting duty about AI-enabled phishing; no type covers phishing vigilance, so UNCOVERED.

units.resolution_why: Only A split this out. The source gives a separate directive, "adhere to security best practices and to report any dubious messages", which is a real instruction to all readers. It is about phishing hygiene, not any listed AI-use type, so UNCOVERED is kept (B folded it into P53, which names harms but does not instruct reporting).

The source adds a condition ("Level 2 or higher in confidentiality") and an approving office that the anchor lacks, so B's normalized policy is kept; phase set to during-work because it governs the act of using a tool. Type P50, should and restrict agree.

The sentence has no named subject and is addressed to anyone acquiring tools ("If you have already obtained, or are contemplating the acquisition ..."), so actor all. Tools may not be used until evaluated, so restrict. P65 and must agree. B's longer policy also merged the purchasing contact rule, which is kept as its own unit; the anchor states the rule alone, so policy is null.

units.why: "Connect with OIT before purchasing any generative AI tools" and "reach out to OIT's AI team" tell anyone buying or planning to buy AI tools to contact OIT first; this is a procurement-review step, P65, should (a directive heading with a conditional invitation), before use.

These are two distinct rules (contact OIT before buying; tools must be risk-evaluated), so one unit each. A's anchor was replaced by the section heading, which states the rule in full.

documents.title: Establishing Course Policies (Student Use of Artificial Intelligence section)
documents.summary: The Center for Teaching and Learning page on establishing course policies includes a section on student AI use. It advises instructors to put an AI statement in the syllabus, treat AI as an extension of collaboration and honesty policies, and decide on documentation and citation, listing questions rather than rules. Only that section was coded.
documents.stance_why: The AI section is a prompt for instructors: "Let your students know your expectations" and a list of questions to consider. It sets no stance and leaves the rule to each instructor, so delegates; it gives no tiers.

units.why: "Let your students know your expectations for how they should collaborate with and cite" tells instructors to state AI expectations in the syllabus: P09.
units.anchor: Let your students know your expectations for how they should collaborate with and cite
units.frag_start: Let your students know your expectations

units.why: "Without including this information in your syllabus, students will not know how" gives the reason for a syllabus AI statement, so P09 informs.
units.anchor: Without including this information in your syllabus, students will not know how
units.frag_start: Without including this information in your syllabus,

units.why: The sentence warns that without a syllabus statement students "may resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants due to fear of penalization"; it is a rationale for stating expectations, so informs, instructor, course-start, P09 (require an AI statement in every syllabus). P18 (prose vs code) does not fit: it does not separate prose from code.
units.anchor: resist using basic GenAI functions such as spelling and grammar assistants
units.frag_start: they may resist using basic GenAI functions
units.resolution_why: Both coders assigned P18. The source sentence gives a consequence of silence on AI in the syllabus; it does not separate AI for prose from AI for code, so P18's definition is not met. It repeats the rationale of the previous unit, so recoded to P09 (informs).

units.why: "consider students' engagement with GenAI as an extension of your collaboration and academic honesty policies" treats AI as collaboration under existing rules: P45.
